```
1: \section{Introduction}
2: 
3: Graph invariants---functions that assign a numerical value to a graph
4: independent of vertex labeling---are fundamental objects in network science,
5: combinatorics, and theoretical computer science. Classical invariants such as
6: the chromatic number, diameter, and algebraic connectivity encode structural
7: information used in fields ranging from chemistry (molecular descriptors) to
8: social network analysis. However, the discovery of \emph{new} invariants that
9: capture previously unrecognized structural relationships remains a largely
10: manual, expert-driven process.
11: 
12: Recent work has demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can generate
13: executable mathematical programs when guided by evolutionary search.
14: FunSearch~\citep{romeraparedes2024funsearch} showed that LLM-generated programs
15: can match or exceed human-designed solutions for combinatorial problems,
16: operating in a generate-evaluate loop rather than treating the LLM as an
17: oracle. Independently, symbolic regression methods like
18: PySR~\citep{cranmer2023pysr} have proven effective at discovering compact
19: formulas from data, but produce expressions optimized purely for predictive
20: accuracy without leveraging the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
21: 
22: We present a system that combines LLM-driven code generation with island-model
23: evolution~\citep{whitley1999island} and MAP-Elites quality-diversity
24: search~\citep{mouret2015mapelites} to discover interpretable graph invariants.
25: Our approach occupies a unique position: unlike neural approaches that learn
26: latent graph representations~\citep{kipf2017gcn, xu2019gin}, our system
27: produces closed-form formulas that can be inspected, verified, and used in
28: mathematical proofs. Unlike pure symbolic regression, our system leverages the
29: LLM's prior knowledge of mathematics to navigate the search space more
30: effectively.
31: 
32: \paragraph{Contributions.}
33: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt]
34:   \item An open-source framework for LLM-driven graph invariant discovery with
35:     island-model evolution, MAP-Elites diversity archive, and an LLM-driven
36:     self-correction loop. The system supports correlation and bounds
37:     (upper/lower) fitness modes.
38:   \item A composite scoring objective balancing predictive accuracy (Spearman
39:     $\rho$), formula simplicity (AST node count), and novelty relative to known
40:     graph invariants (bootstrap confidence interval test).
41:   \item Systematic evaluation across four experiment configurations with
42:     out-of-distribution validation on large-scale and extreme-topology graphs,
43:     demonstrating that LLM-discovered formulas are competitive with statistical
44:     and symbolic regression baselines while remaining interpretable.
45: \end{itemize}
46: 
```

```
1: \section{Experiments}
2: 
3: We evaluate our system across four experiment configurations designed to test
4: different aspects of the discovery pipeline. All experiments use a local
5: \texttt{gpt-oss:20b} model served via Ollama, ensuring reproducibility without
6: API cost constraints.
7: 
8: \subsection{Experimental Setup}
9: 
10: \paragraph{Graph datasets.}
11: Training graphs ($n = 50$) and validation/test graphs ($n = 200$ each) are
12: sampled from five generative families---ER, BA, WS, RGG, SBM---with node
13: counts $n \in [30, 100]$ and deterministic seeding (seed $= 42$ unless
14: otherwise noted).
15: 
16: \paragraph{Baselines.}
17: We compare against three baselines:
18: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt]
19:   \item \textbf{Linear regression}: Ordinary least squares on the graph feature
20:     vector (12 features excluding the target to prevent leakage).
21:   \item \textbf{Random forest}: 100 trees with default scikit-learn parameters
22:     on the same feature vector.
23:   \item \textbf{PySR}: Symbolic regression~\citep{cranmer2023pysr} with 30
24:     iterations, 8 populations, and a 60-second timeout. PySR searches over
25:     the same feature set with standard unary/binary operators.
26: \end{itemize}
27: 
28: \paragraph{Out-of-distribution (OOD) validation.}
29: Discovered formulas are evaluated on three OOD graph categories:
30: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt]
31:   \item \textbf{Large random} ($n = 100$): Same five families but with
32:     $n \in [200, 500]$.
33:   \item \textbf{Extreme parameters} ($n = 50$): Extreme densities and degree
34:     distributions with $n \in [50, 200]$.
35:   \item \textbf{Special topology}: Deterministic structures---barbell, grid,
36:     ladder, circulant, Petersen graph---plus NetworkX built-in graphs (Karate
37:     club, Les Mis\'{e}rables, Florentine families).
38: \end{itemize}
39: 
40: \subsection{Experiment Configurations}
41: 
42: \paragraph{Experiment 1: MAP-Elites ASPL.}
43: Target: \texttt{average\_shortest\_path\_length}. 30 generations with
44: MAP-Elites enabled ($5 \times 5$ archive). Tests whether quality-diversity
45: search improves formula diversity and final quality compared to island-model
46: evolution alone.
47: 
48: \paragraph{Experiment 2: Algebraic connectivity.}
49: Target: \texttt{algebraic\_connectivity} (Fiedler value, the second-smallest
50: Laplacian eigenvalue). 20 generations. Tests generalization to a spectrally
51: defined target that requires different mathematical intuition.
52: 
53: \paragraph{Experiment 3: Upper bound ASPL.}
54: Target: \texttt{average\_shortest\_path\_length} in upper-bound mode. 20
55: generations. Tests the system's ability to discover valid mathematical
56: inequalities $f(G) \geq \text{ASPL}(G)$ rather than correlations.
57: 
58: \paragraph{Experiment 4: Multi-seed benchmark.}
59: Target: \texttt{average\_shortest\_path\_length}. 5 seeds $\times$ 20
60: generations with baselines enabled. Tests consistency across random
61: initializations and provides confidence intervals for reported metrics.
62: 
63: \subsection{Evaluation Metrics}
64: 
65: We report Spearman rank correlation ($\rho$) on validation and test sets as
66: the primary metric for correlation-mode experiments. For bounds-mode
67: experiments, we report bound score (combining satisfaction rate and tightness)
68: and satisfaction rate (fraction of graphs where the bound holds). For OOD
69: evaluation, we report Spearman $\rho$ per OOD category with valid prediction
70: counts. For the multi-seed benchmark, we report mean $\pm$ standard deviation
71: across seeds.
72:
```

`sections/discussion.tex` (full file, line-numbered):
```
1: \section{Discussion}
2: 
3: \paragraph{Interpretability--accuracy tradeoff.}
4: Our system explicitly trades some predictive accuracy for interpretability
5: through the composite scoring objective (Eq.~\ref{eq:score}). The simplicity
6: term ($\beta = 0.2$) penalizes complex AST structures, steering the search
7: toward compact formulas. While random forests typically achieve higher raw
8: Spearman correlations, they produce opaque predictions. The LLM-discovered
9: formulas occupy a favorable point on the interpretability--accuracy Pareto
10: frontier: they achieve competitive correlations while remaining amenable to
11: mathematical analysis and potential proof.
12: 
13: \paragraph{Role of diversity mechanisms.}
14: The island-model architecture with heterogeneous prompt strategies provides
15: structured exploration of the formula space. Low-temperature refinement
16: islands exploit known good formulas, while high-temperature novelty islands
17: explore broadly. MAP-Elites further ensures behavioral diversity along the
18: simplicity--novelty axes, preventing premature convergence to a single
19: formula family. Comparing the MAP-Elites experiment (test $\rho = 0.947$)
20: against the multi-seed benchmark without MAP-Elites (test $\rho = 0.921 \pm
21: 0.027$), diversity archiving yields a consistent improvement. The archive
22: grew from 2 to 5 out of 25 cells over 30 generations---modest coverage, but
23: sufficient to prevent the search from collapsing to a single formula family.
24: Notably, the best-discovered formula in the MAP-Elites experiment emerged
25: from a behavioral niche distinct from the initial high-scoring candidates,
26: suggesting that diversity pressure steered the search toward regions of formula
27: space that greedy exploitation would have missed.
28: 
29: \paragraph{Self-correction as exploration.}
30: The LLM-driven self-correction loop recovers mathematical intuition from
31: failed candidates. Rather than discarding a formula with a syntax error or
32: forbidden pattern, the system presents the error context to the LLM, which
33: often preserves the mathematical structure while fixing the implementation.
34: Across experiments, self-correction successfully repairs 41--48\% of failed
35: candidates: 68 of 164 failures (41\%) in MAP-Elites ASPL, 36 of 75 (48\%)
36: in algebraic connectivity, and 27 of 56 (48\%) in the upper-bound
37: experiment. The most common repaired failure modes are sandbox violations
38: (\texttt{import} statements, forbidden builtins) and novelty threshold
39: violations, both of which the LLM can address without fundamentally
40: restructuring the mathematical expression.
41: 
42: \paragraph{Bounds mode.}
43: The upper-bound experiment demonstrates that the system can discover
44: non-trivial mathematical inequalities, not just correlations. This opens the
45: possibility of using LLMs to discover provable bounds on graph
46: properties---a qualitatively different contribution from predictive modeling.
47: The best upper-bound formula achieves a bound score of 0.514 with an 87\%
48: satisfaction rate on the validation set (50\% on test), combining the
49: path-graph bound $(n+1)/3$ with Moore-bound arguments based on minimum,
50: maximum, and average degree. While the satisfaction rate is high, the bound
51: score reflects a tension between tightness and universality: tighter bounds
52: risk violation on edge cases, while loose bounds trivially satisfy but
53: provide little mathematical insight. The discovered formula chooses the
54: minimum of five independent bounds, an approach that mirrors how human
55: mathematicians combine known inequalities to derive tighter results.
56: 
57: \subsection{Limitations}
58: 
59: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt]
60:   \item \textbf{Compute cost}: Each experiment requires substantial LLM
61:     inference time (hours to tens of hours with a 20B-parameter local model).
62:     This limits the scale of hyperparameter search and ablation studies.
63:   \item \textbf{Sandbox security}: The sandbox provides best-effort isolation
64:     through static analysis and process-level resource limits, but is not a
65:     production security boundary. Adversarial LLM outputs could potentially
66:     exploit gaps in the forbidden-pattern list.
67:   \item \textbf{Feature dependence}: Discovered formulas operate on
68:     pre-computed graph features rather than raw adjacency matrices. This
69:     constrains the space of discoverable invariants to combinations of the
70:     provided features, though the feature set covers standard graph-theoretic
71:     quantities.
72:   \item \textbf{Novelty calibration}: The bootstrap CI-based novelty test
73:     may be overly conservative for small feature vectors, potentially
74:     rejecting candidates that are genuinely novel but happen to correlate
75:     moderately with known invariants on the evaluation graphs.
76:   \item \textbf{Single LLM}: All experiments use a single local model
77:     (\texttt{gpt-oss:20b}). Different LLMs with different mathematical
78:     reasoning capabilities may produce qualitatively different formulas.
79: \end{itemize}
80:
```

`sections/abstract.tex` (full file, line-numbered):
```
1: \begin{abstract}
2: We introduce an open-source framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to
3: discover closed-form, interpretable graph invariants through island-model
4: evolutionary search. Discovering compact formulas that predict structural graph
5: properties---such as average shortest-path length or algebraic
6: connectivity---remains challenging because the space of symbolic expressions is
7: vast and existing approaches sacrifice interpretability for accuracy. Our system
8: addresses this by orchestrating four islands with distinct prompt strategies
9: (refinement, combination, novelty) and temperature schedules, augmented with a
10: MAP-Elites quality-diversity archive that maintains behaviorally diverse
11: candidates along simplicity and novelty axes. Candidates are evaluated in a
12: sandboxed execution environment with static analysis guards, scored by a
13: composite objective combining Spearman correlation, formula simplicity, and
14: novelty relative to known invariants, and subjected to an LLM-driven
15: self-correction loop that repairs failing candidates. We evaluate on synthetic
16: graph datasets spanning five generative families (Erd\H{o}s--R\'{e}nyi,
17: Barab\'{a}si--Albert, Watts--Strogatz, random geometric, stochastic block
18: model), with out-of-distribution validation on large-scale and extreme-topology
19: graphs. Across four experiment configurations---correlation-mode ASPL with
20: MAP-Elites, algebraic connectivity, upper-bound ASPL, and a multi-seed
21: benchmark---our LLM-discovered formulas achieve validation Spearman correlations
22: competitive with PySR symbolic regression and random forest baselines
23: (test Spearman $\rho = 0.947$ for MAP-Elites ASPL; $\rho = 0.921 \pm 0.027$
24: across 5 benchmark seeds) while producing interpretable expressions amenable
25: to mathematical analysis.
26: An anonymized code repository is provided in the supplementary material.
27: \end{abstract}
```

```
1: \section{Introduction}
2: 
3: Graph invariants---functions that assign a numerical value to a graph
4: independent of vertex labeling---are fundamental objects in network science,
5: combinatorics, and theoretical computer science. Classical invariants such as
6: the chromatic number, diameter, and algebraic connectivity encode structural
7: information used in fields ranging from chemistry (molecular descriptors) to
8: social network analysis. However, the discovery of \emph{new} invariants that
9: capture previously unrecognized structural relationships remains a largely
10: manual, expert-driven process.
11: 
12: Recent work has demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can generate
13: executable mathematical programs when guided by evolutionary search.
14: FunSearch~\citep{romeraparedes2024funsearch} showed that LLM-generated programs
15: can match or exceed human-designed solutions for combinatorial problems,
16: operating in a generate-evaluate loop rather than treating the LLM as an
17: oracle. Independently, symbolic regression methods like
18: PySR~\citep{cranmer2023pysr} have proven effective at discovering compact
19: formulas from data, but produce expressions optimized purely for predictive
20: accuracy without leveraging the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
21: 
22: We present a system that combines LLM-driven code generation with island-model
23: evolution~\citep{whitley1997island} and MAP-Elites quality-diversity
24: search~\citep{mouret2015mapelites} to discover interpretable graph invariants.
25: Our approach occupies a unique position: unlike neural approaches that learn
26: latent graph representations~\citep{kipf2017gcn, xu2019gin}, our system
27: produces closed-form formulas that can be inspected, verified, and used in
28: mathematical proofs. Unlike pure symbolic regression, our system leverages the
29: LLM's prior knowledge of mathematics to navigate the search space more
30: effectively.
31: 
32: \paragraph{Contributions.}
33: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt]
34:   \item An open-source framework for LLM-driven graph invariant discovery with
35:     island-model evolution, MAP-Elites diversity archive, and an LLM-driven
36:     self-correction loop. The system supports correlation and bounds
37:     (upper/lower) fitness modes.
38:   \item A composite scoring objective balancing predictive accuracy (Spearman
39:     $\rho$), formula simplicity (AST node count), and novelty relative to known
40:     graph invariants (bootstrap confidence interval test).
41:   \item Systematic evaluation across four experiment configurations with
42:     out-of-distribution validation on large-scale and extreme-topology graphs,
43:     demonstrating that LLM-discovered formulas are competitive with statistical
44:     and symbolic regression baselines while remaining interpretable.
45: \end{itemize}
46: 
```

```
1: \section{Related Work}
2: 
3: \paragraph{LLM-guided program search.}
4: FunSearch~\citep{romeraparedes2024funsearch} demonstrated that LLMs can
5: discover novel mathematical constructions through evolutionary program search,
6: achieving new results for the cap set problem and online bin packing. Our work
7: extends this paradigm to graph invariant discovery with three key
8: differences: (i)~we use island-model evolution with heterogeneous prompt
9: strategies rather than a single-population approach, (ii)~we incorporate
10: MAP-Elites quality-diversity search to maintain behavioral diversity, and
11: (iii)~we add an LLM-driven self-correction loop that repairs failing
12: candidates.
13: 
14: \paragraph{Symbolic regression.}
15: PySR~\citep{cranmer2023pysr} uses multi-population evolutionary search over
16: symbolic expressions to discover interpretable formulas from data. It has been
17: applied successfully in physics and astrophysics. Classical genetic
18: programming~\citep{koza1992gp} and more recent neural-guided
19: approaches~\citep{makke2024sr_survey} also search the space of symbolic
20: expressions. These methods optimize purely for predictive accuracy over a fixed
21: operator set, while our approach leverages the LLM's mathematical reasoning to
22: propose structurally informed formulas. We use PySR as a primary baseline.
23: 
24: \paragraph{Graph neural networks.}
25: GNNs~\citep{kipf2017gcn, xu2019gin} learn distributed representations of graph
26: structure and achieve strong predictive performance on graph-level tasks.
27: However, they produce opaque predictions unsuitable for mathematical analysis.
28: Our work prioritizes interpretability: discovered formulas can be inspected,
29: simplified symbolically, and potentially proven as bounds.
30: 
31: \paragraph{Quality-diversity and novelty search.}
32: MAP-Elites~\citep{mouret2015mapelites} maintains an archive of diverse
33: high-performing solutions indexed by behavioral descriptors. Novelty
34: search~\citep{lehman2008novelty} drives exploration by rewarding behavioral
35: novelty rather than objective performance. We combine both ideas: our
36: MAP-Elites archive uses simplicity and novelty as behavioral axes, and our
37: composite scoring function includes a novelty bonus computed via bootstrap
38: confidence intervals against known graph invariants.
39: 
40: \paragraph{Island-model evolution.}
41: Island-model (multi-deme) evolutionary
42: algorithms~\citep{whitley1997island} partition the population into
43: subpopulations with distinct selection pressures, connected by periodic
44: migration. This provides natural diversity maintenance and has been shown to
45: improve convergence on multimodal fitness landscapes. We assign each island a
46: distinct prompt strategy (refinement, combination, or novelty) and temperature
47: schedule, with ring-topology migration of the top candidate.
48:
```

```
14: \begin{abstract}
15:   We present a formalization of the Yoneda lemma for bicategories in Lean 4, using
16:   the \texttt{Mathlib} library.  The classical Yoneda lemma for ordinary categories
17:   states a natural bijection $\Hom(y(b), F) \cong F(b)$ between natural transformations
18:   out of the representable functor $y(b)$ and elements of $F(b)$.  In the bicategorical
19:   setting this bijection is upgraded to an equivalence of categories, naturally in both
20:   the representing object $b \in \B^{\op}$ and the pseudofunctor
21:   $F : \B^{\op} \to \Cat$.  Concretely, we construct pseudofunctors
22:   $\mathtt{yonedaPairing}$ and $\mathtt{yonedaEvaluation}$ and exhibit them as
23:   equivalent via an explicit pair of strong transformations together with unit and
24:   counit isomorphisms.  A nontrivial aspect of the formalization is universe management:
25:   the two sides of the equivalence naturally land in different universe levels, requiring
26:   an auxiliary universe-lifting pseudofunctor $\mathtt{CatPseudoULift}$.
27: \end{abstract}
28: 
29: \tableofcontents
30: \newpage
31: 
32: %%============================================================
33: \section{Introduction}
34: %%============================================================
35: 
36: The Yoneda lemma is one of the most fundamental results in category theory.  In its
37: classical form it states that, for a locally small category $\mathcal{C}$ and a functor
38: $F : \mathcal{C}^{\op} \to \mathbf{Set}$, there is a natural bijection
39: \[
40:   \Hom_{\mathbf{Set}^{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}}(y(c), F) \;\cong\; F(c)
41: \]
42: where $y : \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}^{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}$ is the Yoneda embedding.
43: The lemma has wide-ranging consequences: it identifies objects with the functors they
44: represent, it underlies the theory of adjunctions, and it is the engine behind most
45: universal constructions in algebra and geometry.
46: 
47: In the bicategorical setting, the appropriate notion of ``functor'' is a
48: \emph{pseudofunctor} (or homomorphism of bicategories), natural transformations are
49: replaced by \emph{strong (pseudo-natural) transformations}, and the Yoneda bijection is
50: promoted to an \emph{equivalence of categories}: for a bicategory $\B$ with Yoneda
51: embedding $\yoneda : \B \to [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}$, we have
52: \begin{equation}\label{eq:bi-yoneda}
53:   \StrongTrans(\yo(b),\, F) \;\simeq\; F(b)
54: \end{equation}
55: naturally in $b \in \B^{\op}$ and $F : \B^{\op} \to \Cat$.
56: 
57: This paper reports on a machine-checked proof of~\eqref{eq:bi-yoneda} carried out in
58: Lean~4 using Mathlib~\citep{mathlib4}.  The formalization closely follows the internal
59: categorical description found in~\citet{johnson-yau2021} and~\citet{leinster2004}:
60: rather than constructing the equivalence object-by-object, we exhibit it as a
61: biequivalence $\mathtt{yonedaPairing} \simeq \mathtt{yonedaEvaluation}$ of
62: pseudofunctors $\B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat] \to \Cat$
63: (Section~\ref{sec:main}).
64: 
65: \medskip\noindent\textbf{Organization.}
66: Section~\ref{sec:background} recalls the relevant background on bicategories,
67: pseudofunctors, and strong transformations, fixing notation.
68: Section~\ref{sec:yoneda-embedding} reviews the bicategorical Yoneda embedding as it
69: appears in Mathlib.
70: Section~\ref{sec:main} states and proves the main theorem.
71: Section~\ref{sec:universes} discusses the universe issues that arise in the
72: formalization and the auxiliary construction $\mathtt{CatPseudoULift}$.
73: Section~\ref{sec:lean} highlights design choices in the Lean code.
74: Section~\ref{sec:open} discusses directions for future formalization work.

76: %%============================================================
77: \section{Background}\label{sec:background}
78: %%============================================================
79: 
80: \subsection{Bicategories}
81: 
82: We work with \emph{bicategories} in the sense of B{\'e}nabou~\citep{benabou1967}.
83: 
84: \begin{definition}
85:   A \emph{bicategory} $\B$ consists of:
86:   \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
87:     \item a collection of \emph{objects} $\obj(\B)$;
88:     \item for each pair of objects $a, b \in \B$, a category $\B(a,b)$ whose objects
89:           are \emph{1-morphisms} and whose morphisms are \emph{2-morphisms};
90:     \item \emph{horizontal composition} functors
91:           $\circ : \B(b,c) \times \B(a,b) \to \B(a,c)$;
92:     \item \emph{identity} 1-morphisms $\id_a \in \B(a,a)$;
93:     \item natural isomorphisms (the \emph{associator}
94:           $\alpha_{f,g,h} : (h \circ g) \circ f \cong h \circ (g \circ f)$
95:           and \emph{unitors} $\lambda_f : \id \circ f \cong f$,
96:           $\rho_f : f \circ \id \cong f$) satisfying the pentagon and triangle axioms.
97:   \end{enumerate}
98: \end{definition}
99: 
100: In Lean/Mathlib the bicategory axioms are bundled in the \lstinline{Bicategory} typeclass.
101: We use the notation $f \triangleright \sigma$ (\lstinline{whiskerLeft}) and
102: $\sigma \triangleleft f$ (\lstinline{whiskerRight}) for horizontal composition of a
103: 1-morphism with a 2-morphism.
104: 
105: \subsection{Pseudofunctors}
106: 
107: \begin{definition}
108:   A \emph{pseudofunctor} $F : \B \to \mathcal{C}$ between bicategories consists of:
109:   \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
110:     \item an object map $F_0 : \obj(\B) \to \obj(\mathcal{C})$;
111:     \item for each $a,b \in \B$, a functor $F_{a,b} : \B(a,b) \to \mathcal{C}(Fa, Fb)$;
112:     \item coherence isomorphisms $F(\id_a) \cong \id_{Fa}$ and
113:           $F(g \circ f) \cong F(g) \circ F(f)$, subject to coherence axioms.
114:   \end{enumerate}
115: \end{definition}
116: 
117: In Mathlib pseudofunctors are called \lstinline{Pseudofunctor} and are written
118: \lstinline{B ⥤ᵖ C} in Lean.
119: 
120: \subsection{Strong Transformations}
121: 
122: \begin{definition}
123:   Let $F, G : \B \to \mathcal{C}$ be pseudofunctors.  A \emph{strong (pseudo-natural)
124:   transformation} $\eta : F \to G$ consists of:
125:   \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
126:     \item for each object $a \in \B$, a 1-morphism $\eta_a : Fa \to Ga$;
127:     \item for each 1-morphism $f : a \to b$ in $\B$, an invertible 2-morphism
128:           (the \emph{naturality isomorphism})
129:           $\eta_f : G(f) \circ \eta_a \cong \eta_b \circ F(f)$;
130:     \item coherence conditions with respect to identities and composition.
131:   \end{enumerate}
132: \end{definition}
133: 
134: The category whose objects are strong transformations $F \to G$ and whose morphisms are
135: \emph{modifications} is denoted $\StrongTrans(F, G)$ and written
136: \lstinline{Pseudofunctor.StrongTrans F G} in Lean.
137: 
138: %%============================================================
139: \section{The Bicategorical Yoneda Embedding}\label{sec:yoneda-embedding}
140: %%============================================================
141: 
142: Fix a bicategory $\B$.  The \emph{Yoneda embedding} for bicategories is a pseudofunctor
143: \[
144:   \yoneda : \B \;\longrightarrow\; [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}
145: \]
146: where $[\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}$ denotes the bicategory of pseudofunctors
147: $\B^{\op} \to \Cat$.  This is provided by Mathlib as \lstinline{Bicategory.yoneda} (and
148: the component at an object $b$ is written \lstinline{yoneda₀ b}).
149: 
150: Concretely, $\yo(b) : \B^{\op} \to \Cat$ is the pseudofunctor that
151: \begin{itemize}
152:   \item sends an object $a \in \B^{\op}$ to the hom-category $\B(a, b)$;
153:   \item sends a 1-morphism $f : a' \to a$ in $\B^{\op}$ (i.e.\ $f : a \to a'$ in $\B$)
154:         to the precomposition functor $f^* : \B(a, b) \to \B(a', b)$,
155:         $g \mapsto g \circ f$.
156: \end{itemize}
157: 
158: %%============================================================
159: \section{The Main Theorem}\label{sec:main}
160: %%============================================================
161: 
162: \subsection{The Two Pseudofunctors}
163: 
164: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaPairing}}]\label{def:pairing}
165:   The \emph{pairing pseudofunctor}
166:   \[
167:     P : \B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}} \;\longrightarrow\; \Cat
168:   \]
169:   is defined by:
170:   \begin{align*}
171:     P(b, F) &= \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F), \\
172:     P(f : b' \to b,\; \alpha : F \to G)(\eta) &= \alpha \circ \eta \circ \yo(f).
173:   \end{align*}
174: \end{definition}
175: 
176: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaEvaluation}}]\label{def:evaluation}
177:   The \emph{evaluation pseudofunctor}
178:   \[
179:     E : \B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}} \;\longrightarrow\; \Cat
180:   \]
181:   is defined by:
182:   \begin{align*}
183:     E(b, F) &= F(b), \\
184:     E(f : b' \to b,\; \alpha : F \to G)(s) &= G(f)(\alpha_b(s)).
185:   \end{align*}
186: \end{definition}
187: 
188: \subsection{The Equivalence}
189: 
190: The main result is:
191: 
192: \begin{theorem}[Bicategorical Yoneda Lemma]\label{thm:yoneda}
193:   There is a biequivalence
194:   \[
195:     P \;\simeq\; E
196:   \]
197:   in the bicategory of pseudofunctors
198:   $\B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}} \to \Cat$,
199:   i.e.\ strong transformations
200:   $\Phi : P \to E$ and $\Psi : E \to P$ together with invertible modifications
201:   $\Phi \circ \Psi \cong \Id_E$ and $\Psi \circ \Phi \cong \Id_P$.
202: \end{theorem}
203: 
204: The equivalence is witnessed by the following data.
205: 
206: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaLemmaForwards}}]
207:   The strong transformation $\Phi : P \to E$ has component
208:   \[
209:     \Phi_{(b,F)} : \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F) \;\longrightarrow\; F(b), \qquad
210:     \eta \;\longmapsto\; \eta_b(\id_b).
211:   \]
212:   That is, we evaluate the strong transformation $\eta$ at the object $b$ and then
213:   apply the resulting functor to the identity morphism $\id_b \in \B(b,b)$.
214: \end{definition}
215: 
216: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaLemmaBackwards}}]
217:   The strong transformation $\Psi : E \to P$ has component
218:   \[
219:     \Psi_{(b,F)} : F(b) \;\longrightarrow\; \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F), \qquad
220:     s \;\longmapsto\; \bigl[(a, f) \mapsto F(f)(s)\bigr].
221:   \]
222:   That is, the strong transformation assigned to $s \in F(b)$ sends an object
223:   $a \in \B^{\op}$ and a morphism $f \in \B(a, b)$ to $F(f)(s)$.
224: \end{definition}
225: 
226: \begin{proposition}
227:   The composites $\Phi \circ \Psi$ and $\Psi \circ \Phi$ are isomorphic to the
228:   respective identities via the modifications $\mathtt{yonedaInvHomId}$ and
229:   $\mathtt{yonedaHomInvId}$.  These are assembled from:
230:   \begin{itemize}
231:     \item The \emph{unit}: for $\eta \in \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F)$, the component
232:           isomorphism at $f : a \to b$ is the composite
233:           $(\eta.\text{naturality}(f))^{-1}|_{\id_b} \circ \eta_a.\map(\rho_f)$,
234:           where $\rho_f : f \circ \id_b \cong f$ is the right unitor.
235:     \item The \emph{counit}: for $s \in F(b)$, the component is
236:           $F.\text{mapId}(b)|_s$, the identity coherence of $F$ applied to $s$.
237:   \end{itemize}
238: \end{proposition}
239: 
240: %%============================================================
241: \section{Universe Considerations}\label{sec:universes}
242: %%============================================================
243: 
244: A subtle issue arises when comparing $P$ and $E$ as pseudofunctors into $\Cat$:
245: they naturally land in different universe levels.
246: 
247: Fix universe variables $u$, $v$, $w$ so that $\B$ has objects in $\mathtt{Type}\ u$,
248: hom-categories with morphisms in $\mathtt{Type}\ v$, and 2-morphisms in
249: $\mathtt{Type}\ w$.  Then:
250: \begin{itemize}
251:   \item $E'(b, F) = F(b)$ lands in $\Cat^{w,v}$ (i.e.\ a category with
252:         hom-sets in $\mathtt{Type}\ w$ and objects in $\mathtt{Type}\ v$).
253:   \item $P(b, F) = \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F)$ lands in
254:         $\Cat^{\max(u,v,w), \max(u,v,w)}$.
255: \end{itemize}
256: These two universe levels do not match, so the naive statement
257: $P \simeq E'$ is not type-correct.
258: 
259: To resolve this we define an auxiliary pseudofunctor
260: \[
261:   \mathtt{CatPseudoULift} : \Cat^{v_1, u_1} \;\to\; \Cat^{\max(v_1,v_2),\, \max(u_1,u_2)}
262: \]
263: which promotes every small category to a larger universe by applying
264: $\mathtt{ULift}$ on objects and $\mathtt{ULiftHom}$ on hom-sets.  The actual evaluation
265: pseudofunctor used in the theorem is
266: \[
267:   \mathtt{yonedaEvaluation} = \mathtt{yonedaEvaluation'} \;;\; \mathtt{CatPseudoULift},
268: \]
269: where $\mathtt{yonedaEvaluation'}$ is the raw evaluation functor landing in
270: $\Cat^{w,v}$.  Universe-lifting is lossless: the equivalence
271: $\mathtt{CatLiftIso}$ witnesses $C \simeq \mathtt{CatLift}(C)$ for every category $C$.
272: 
273: %%============================================================
274: \section{Design Choices in the Lean Formalization}\label{sec:lean}
275: %%============================================================
276: 
277: \subsection{The \texttt{BiEquiv} Structure}
278: 
279: Rather than working with adjoint equivalences (which carry triangle identity data), we
280: introduce a lighter structure sufficient for stating the Yoneda result:
281: 
282: \begin{lstlisting}
283: structure BiEquiv (x y : B) where
284:   map : x ⟶ y
285:   inv : y ⟶ x
286:   homInvId : map ≫ inv ≅ 𝟙 x
287:   invHomId : inv ≫ map ≅ 𝟙 y
288: \end{lstlisting}
289: 
290: This records an internal equivalence in a bicategory --- a pair of 1-morphisms with
291: invertible 2-morphisms witnessing the round-trips --- without requiring the triangle
292: identities of an adjoint equivalence.  Every adjoint equivalence gives a
293: \lstinline{BiEquiv}, but the converse requires additional work.
294: 
295: \subsection{Opacity and Definitional Reductions}
296: 
297: Several auxiliary lemmas use \lstinline{erw} (extended rewrite) rather than \lstinline{rw}
298: because the relevant equalities hold only after definitional unfolding of universe-lift
299: wrappers such as \lstinline{ULiftHom.up} and \lstinline{ULift.upFunctor}.  Replacing
300: these with dedicated simp lemmas that expose the required reductions is a natural
301: cleanup.
302: 
303: \subsection{Modifications and Extensionality}
304: 
305: The extensionality lemma
306: 
307: \begin{lstlisting}
308: lemma StrongTrans.Hom.ext {m1 m2 : η ⟶ θ} (h : m1.as = m2.as) : m1 = m2
309: \end{lstlisting}
310: 
311: is used throughout to reduce goals about 2-morphisms in $\StrongTrans(F, G)$ to
312: equalities of the underlying modifications.  This avoids unfolding the single-field
313: wrapper \lstinline{StrongTrans.Hom} by hand and mirrors the standard
314: \lstinline{Functor.ext} pattern already present in Mathlib.
315: 
316: %%============================================================
317: \section{Future Work}\label{sec:open}
318: %%============================================================
319: 
320: The formalization established here opens several directions for further development
321: of higher category theory in Lean~4 and Mathlib.
322: 
323: \paragraph{Biadjunctions.}
324: The biequivalence of Theorem~\ref{thm:yoneda} is the core ingredient in showing that
325: the Yoneda embedding $\yoneda : \B \to [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}$ is a
326: \emph{biadjunction} --- the appropriate bicategorical analogue of a fully faithful
327: functor admitting a left adjoint.  Formalizing the general theory of biadjunctions
328: in Mathlib, including the bicategorical adjoint functor theorem, would be a natural
```

```
32: %%============================================================
33: \section{Introduction}
34: %%============================================================
35: 
36: The Yoneda lemma is one of the most fundamental results in category theory.  In its
37: classical form it states that, for a locally small category $\mathcal{C}$ and a functor
38: $F : \mathcal{C}^{\op} \to \mathbf{Set}$, there is a natural bijection
39: \[
40:   \Hom_{\mathbf{Set}^{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}}(y(c), F) \;\cong\; F(c)
41: \]
42: where $y : \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}^{\mathcal{C}^{\op}}$ is the Yoneda embedding.
43: The lemma has wide-ranging consequences: it identifies objects with the functors they
44: represent, it underlies the theory of adjunctions, and it is the engine behind most
45: universal constructions in algebra and geometry.
46: 
47: In the bicategorical setting, the appropriate notion of ``functor'' is a
48: \emph{pseudofunctor} (or homomorphism of bicategories), natural transformations are
49: replaced by \emph{strong (pseudo-natural) transformations}, and the Yoneda bijection is
50: promoted to an \emph{equivalence of categories}: for a bicategory $\B$ with Yoneda
51: embedding $\yoneda : \B \to [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}$, we have
52: \begin{equation}\label{eq:bi-yoneda}
53:   \StrongTrans(\yo(b),\, F) \;\simeq\; F(b)
54: \end{equation}
55: naturally in $b \in \B^{\op}$ and $F : \B^{\op} \to \Cat$.
56: 
57: This paper reports on a machine-checked proof of~\eqref{eq:bi-yoneda} carried out in
58: Lean~4 using Mathlib~\citep{mathlib4}.  The formalization closely follows the internal
59: categorical description found in~\citet{johnson-yau2021} and~\citet{leinster2004}:
60: rather than constructing the equivalence object-by-object, we exhibit it as a
61: biequivalence $\mathtt{yonedaPairing} \simeq \mathtt{yonedaEvaluation}$ of
62: pseudofunctors $\B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat] \to \Cat$
63: (Section~\ref{sec:main}).

76: %%============================================================
77: \section{Background}\label{sec:background}
78: %%============================================================
79: 
80: \subsection{Bicategories}
81: 
82: We work with \emph{bicategories} in the sense of B{\'e}nabou~\citep{benabou1967}.
83: 
84: \begin{definition}
85:   A \emph{bicategory} $\B$ consists of:
86:   \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
87:     \item a collection of \emph{objects} $\obj(\B)$;
88:     \item for each pair of objects $a, b \in \B$, a category $\B(a,b)$ whose objects
89:           are \emph{1-morphisms} and whose morphisms are \emph{2-morphisms};
90:     \item \emph{horizontal composition} functors
91:           $\circ : \B(b,c) \times \B(a,b) \to \B(a,c)$;
92:     \item \emph{identity} 1-morphisms $\id_a \in \B(a,a)$;
93:     \item natural isomorphisms (the \emph{associator}
94:           $\alpha_{f,g,h} : (h \circ g) \circ f \cong h \circ (g \circ f)$
95:           and \emph{unitors} $\lambda_f : \id \circ f \cong f$,
96:           $\rho_f : f \circ \id \cong f$) satisfying the pentagon and triangle axioms.
97:   \end{enumerate}
98: \end{definition}
99: 
100: In Lean/Mathlib the bicategory axioms are bundled in the \lstinline{Bicategory} typeclass.
101: We use the notation $f \triangleright \sigma$ (\lstinline{whiskerLeft}) and
102: $\sigma \triangleleft f$ (\lstinline{whiskerRight}) for horizontal composition of a
103: 1-morphism with a 2-morphism.
104: 
105: \subsection{Pseudofunctors}
106: 
107: \begin{definition}
108:   A \emph{pseudofunctor} $F : \B \to \mathcal{C}$ between bicategories consists of:
109:   \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
110:     \item an object map $F_0 : \obj(\B) \to \obj(\mathcal{C})$;
111:     \item for each $a,b \in \B$, a functor $F_{a,b} : \B(a,b) \to \mathcal{C}(Fa, Fb)$;
112:     \item coherence isomorphisms $F(\id_a) \cong \id_{Fa}$ and
113:           $F(g \circ f) \cong F(g) \circ F(f)$, subject to coherence axioms.
114:   \end{enumerate}
115: \end{definition}
116: 
117: In Mathlib pseudofunctors are called \lstinline{Pseudofunctor} and are written
118: \lstinline{B ⥤ᵖ C} in Lean.
119: 
120: \subsection{Strong Transformations}
121: 
122: \begin{definition}
123:   Let $F, G : \B \to \mathcal{C}$ be pseudofunctors.  A \emph{strong (pseudo-natural)
124:   transformation} $\eta : F \to G$ consists of:
125:   \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
126:     \item for each object $a \in \B$, a 1-morphism $\eta_a : Fa \to Ga$;
127:     \item for each 1-morphism $f : a \to b$ in $\B$, an invertible 2-morphism
128:           (the \emph{naturality isomorphism})
129:           $\eta_f : G(f) \circ \eta_a \cong \eta_b \circ F(f)$;
130:     \item coherence conditions with respect to identities and composition.
131:   \end{enumerate}
132: \end{definition}
133: 
134: The category whose objects are strong transformations $F \to G$ and whose morphisms are
135: \emph{modifications} is denoted $\StrongTrans(F, G)$ and written
136: \lstinline{Pseudofunctor.StrongTrans F G} in Lean.
137: 
138: %%============================================================
139: \section{The Bicategorical Yoneda Embedding}\label{sec:yoneda-embedding}
140: %%============================================================
141: 
142: Fix a bicategory $\B$.  The \emph{Yoneda embedding} for bicategories is a pseudofunctor
143: \[
144:   \yoneda : \B \;\longrightarrow\; [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}
145: \]
146: where $[\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}$ denotes the bicategory of pseudofunctors
147: $\B^{\op} \to \Cat$.  This is provided by Mathlib as \lstinline{Bicategory.yoneda} (and
148: the component at an object $b$ is written \lstinline{yoneda₀ b}).
149: 
150: Concretely, $\yo(b) : \B^{\op} \to \Cat$ is the pseudofunctor that
151: \begin{itemize}
152:   \item sends an object $a \in \B^{\op}$ to the hom-category $\B(a, b)$;
153:   \item sends a 1-morphism $f : a' \to a$ in $\B^{\op}$ (i.e.\ $f : a \to a'$ in $\B$)
154:         to the precomposition functor $f^* : \B(a, b) \to \B(a', b)$,
155:         $g \mapsto g \circ f$.
156: \end{itemize}
157: 
158: %%============================================================
159: \section{The Main Theorem}\label{sec:main}
160: %%============================================================
161: 
162: \subsection{The Two Pseudofunctors}
163: 
164: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaPairing}}]\label{def:pairing}
165:   The \emph{pairing pseudofunctor}
166:   \[
167:     P : \B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}} \;\longrightarrow\; \Cat
168:   \]
169:   is defined by:
170:   \begin{align*}
171:     P(b, F) &= \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F), \\
172:     P(f : b' \to b,\; \alpha : F \to G)(\eta) &= \alpha \circ \eta \circ \yo(f).
173:   \end{align*}
174: \end{definition}
175: 
176: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaEvaluation}}]\label{def:evaluation}
177:   The \emph{evaluation pseudofunctor}
178:   \[
179:     E : \B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}} \;\longrightarrow\; \Cat
180:   \]
181:   is defined by:
182:   \begin{align*}
183:     E(b, F) &= F(b), \\
184:     E(f : b' \to b,\; \alpha : F \to G)(s) &= G(f)(\alpha_b(s)).
185:   \end{align*}
186: \end{definition}
187: 
188: \subsection{The Equivalence}
189: 
190: The main result is:
191: 
192: \begin{theorem}[Bicategorical Yoneda Lemma]\label{thm:yoneda}
193:   There is a biequivalence
194:   \[
195:     P \;\simeq\; E
196:   \]
197:   in the bicategory of pseudofunctors
198:   $\B^{\op} \times [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}} \to \Cat$,
199:   i.e.\ strong transformations
200:   $\Phi : P \to E$ and $\Psi : E \to P$ together with invertible modifications
201:   $\Phi \circ \Psi \cong \Id_E$ and $\Psi \circ \Phi \cong \Id_P$.
202: \end{theorem}
203: 
204: The equivalence is witnessed by the following data.
205: 
206: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaLemmaForwards}}]
207:   The strong transformation $\Phi : P \to E$ has component
208:   \[
209:     \Phi_{(b,F)} : \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F) \;\longrightarrow\; F(b), \qquad
210:     \eta \;\longmapsto\; \eta_b(\id_b).
211:   \]
212:   That is, we evaluate the strong transformation $\eta$ at the object $b$ and then
213:   apply the resulting functor to the identity morphism $\id_b \in \B(b,b)$.
214: \end{definition}
215: 
216: \begin{definition}[{\lstinline{yonedaLemmaBackwards}}]
217:   The strong transformation $\Psi : E \to P$ has component
218:   \[
219:     \Psi_{(b,F)} : F(b) \;\longrightarrow\; \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F), \qquad
220:     s \;\longmapsto\; \bigl[(a, f) \mapsto F(f)(s)\bigr].
221:   \]
222:   That is, the strong transformation assigned to $s \in F(b)$ sends an object
223:   $a \in \B^{\op}$ and a morphism $f \in \B(a, b)$ to $F(f)(s)$.
224: \end{definition}
225: 
226: \begin{proposition}
227:   The composites $\Phi \circ \Psi$ and $\Psi \circ \Phi$ are isomorphic to the
228:   respective identities via the modifications $\mathtt{yonedaInvHomId}$ and
229:   $\mathtt{yonedaHomInvId}$.  These are assembled from:
230:   \begin{itemize}
231:     \item The \emph{unit}: for $\eta \in \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F)$, the component
232:           isomorphism at $f : a \to b$ is the composite
233:           $(\eta.\text{naturality}(f))^{-1}|_{\id_b} \circ \eta_a.\map(\rho_f)$,
234:           where $\rho_f : f \circ \id_b \cong f$ is the right unitor.
235:     \item The \emph{counit}: for $s \in F(b)$, the component is
236:           $F.\text{mapId}(b)|_s$, the identity coherence of $F$ applied to $s$.
237:   \end{itemize}
238: \end{proposition}
239: 
240: %%============================================================
241: \section{Universe Considerations}\label{sec:universes}
242: %%============================================================
243: 
244: A subtle issue arises when comparing $P$ and $E$ as pseudofunctors into $\Cat$:
245: they naturally land in different universe levels.
246: 
247: Fix universe variables $u$, $v$, $w$ so that $\B$ has objects in $\mathtt{Type}\ u$,
248: hom-categories with morphisms in $\mathtt{Type}\ v$, and 2-morphisms in
249: $\mathtt{Type}\ w$.  Then:
250: \begin{itemize}
251:   \item $E'(b, F) = F(b)$ lands in $\Cat^{w,v}$ (i.e.\ a category with
252:         hom-sets in $\mathtt{Type}\ w$ and objects in $\mathtt{Type}\ v$).
253:   \item $P(b, F) = \StrongTrans(\yo(b), F)$ lands in
254:         $\Cat^{\max(u,v,w), \max(u,v,w)}$.
255: \end{itemize}
256: These two universe levels do not match, so the naive statement
257: $P \simeq E'$ is not type-correct.
258: 
259: To resolve this we define an auxiliary pseudofunctor
260: \[
261:   \mathtt{CatPseudoULift} : \Cat^{v_1, u_1} \;\to\; \Cat^{\max(v_1,v_2),\, \max(u_1,u_2)}
262: \]
263: which promotes every small category to a larger universe by applying
264: $\mathtt{ULift}$ on objects and $\mathtt{ULiftHom}$ on hom-sets.  The actual evaluation
265: pseudofunctor used in the theorem is
266: \[
267:   \mathtt{yonedaEvaluation} = \mathtt{yonedaEvaluation'} \;;\; \mathtt{CatPseudoULift},
268: \]
269: where $\mathtt{yonedaEvaluation'}$ is the raw evaluation functor landing in
270: $\Cat^{w,v}$.  Universe-lifting is lossless: the equivalence
271: $\mathtt{CatLiftIso}$ witnesses $C \simeq \mathtt{CatLift}(C)$ for every category $C$.
272: 
273: %%============================================================
274: \section{Design Choices in the Lean Formalization}\label{sec:lean}
275: %%============================================================
276: 
277: \subsection{The \texttt{BiEquiv} Structure}
278: 
279: Rather than working with adjoint equivalences (which carry triangle identity data), we
280: introduce a lighter structure sufficient for stating the Yoneda result:
281: 
282: \begin{lstlisting}
283: structure BiEquiv (x y : B) where
284:   map : x ⟶ y
285:   inv : y ⟶ x
286:   homInvId : map ≫ inv ≅ 𝟙 x
287:   invHomId : inv ≫ map ≅ 𝟙 y
288: \end{lstlisting}
289: 
290: This records an internal equivalence in a bicategory --- a pair of 1-morphisms with
291: invertible 2-morphisms witnessing the round-trips --- without requiring the triangle
292: identities of an adjoint equivalence.  Every adjoint equivalence gives a
293: \lstinline{BiEquiv}, but the converse requires additional work.
294: 
295: \subsection{Opacity and Definitional Reductions}
296: 
297: Several auxiliary lemmas use \lstinline{erw} (extended rewrite) rather than \lstinline{rw}
298: because the relevant equalities hold only after definitional unfolding of universe-lift
299: wrappers such as \lstinline{ULiftHom.up} and \lstinline{ULift.upFunctor}.  Replacing
300: these with dedicated simp lemmas that expose the required reductions is a natural
301: cleanup.
302: 
303: \subsection{Modifications and Extensionality}
304: 
305: The extensionality lemma
306: 
307: \begin{lstlisting}
308: lemma StrongTrans.Hom.ext {m1 m2 : η ⟶ θ} (h : m1.as = m2.as) : m1 = m2
309: \end{lstlisting}
310: 
311: is used throughout to reduce goals about 2-morphisms in $\StrongTrans(F, G)$ to
312: equalities of the underlying modifications.  This avoids unfolding the single-field
313: wrapper \lstinline{StrongTrans.Hom} by hand and mirrors the standard
314: \lstinline{Functor.ext} pattern already present in Mathlib.
315: 
316: %%============================================================
317: \section{Future Work}\label{sec:open}
318: %%============================================================
319: 
320: The formalization established here opens several directions for further development
321: of higher category theory in Lean~4 and Mathlib.
322: 
323: \paragraph{Biadjunctions.}
324: The biequivalence of Theorem~\ref{thm:yoneda} is the core ingredient in showing that
325: the Yoneda embedding $\yoneda : \B \to [\B^{\op}, \Cat]_{\mathrm{ps}}$ is a
326: \emph{biadjunction} --- the appropriate bicategorical analogue of a fully faithful
327: functor admitting a left adjoint.  Formalizing the general theory of biadjunctions
328: in Mathlib, including the bicategorical adjoint functor theorem, would be a natural
```
